summary:
Carlos Sanchez, principal scientist at Adobe Experience Manager, presents 'Agentic Sites' as real-time, intent-driven personalization that customizes individual blocks—hero, product lists, blog feeds, navigation, CTAs—rather than regenerating whole pages. Strict brand guidelines and rejection of hallucinated content drive a design where the whole site acts as a corpus: a RAG index grounds generated copy against it, while Adobe's edge delivery pairs with backend LLM services such as Cerebras, Bedrock, and others. Model selection is treated as a per-site question and evaluated continuously with Promptfoo, scoring both accuracy and latency because pages must render in one to two seconds or conversions are lost; on the 15-prompt example site Cerebras running Gemma 4 averaged 1.1s versus 4.6s for the runner-up, with throughput around 2,200–2,300 tokens per second. The live coffee-machine demo showed persona-based signal collection feeding a 'For You' page and an on-demand query for a camping coffee machine producing customized hero copy and product recommendations in roughly 1.64s.

The new section introduces OfOneLabs, a tool that generates an agentic site for any URL in under an hour, demonstrated on the AI Engineer site, where a query for 'Europe AI conferences' produced an AI-generated suggestion set and a focused page, and another query yielded a side-by-side conference comparison on the fly. Sanchez projects this personalization beyond the browser—via personal assistants on Google TV and voice surfaces—and argues it will only become faster, cheaper, and more capable, supporting intent-driven assembly of pages for individual users across multiple models.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: What an Agentic Site is trying to do
sections.summary: Sanchez introduces himself as a principal scientist at Adobe Experience Manager and frames Agentic Sites as real-time, intent-driven personalization that customizes sections of a page for the current user to drive engagement or conversions. The stack pairs Adobe edge delivery with backend LLM services (Cerebras featured, plus Bedrock and others), and only certain blocks are personalized while the whole site serves as a corpus via RAG to keep output on-brand.

sections.title: Personalizing blocks, not whole pages
sections.summary: Because marketers enforce strict brand guidelines and reject hallucinations, the system personalizes specific blocks—hero card, products, blog feeds, navigation, CTAs—rather than regenerating the whole site. The example product site includes guides, experiences, and blocks, with comparisons and product pages that can be tailored to the user.

sections.title: Grounding generation in the site itself
sections.summary: The architecture is a dynamic front end of blocks updated in real time by AI, with the back end handling model and provider evaluation. Generation is grounded in a RAG index built from the site itself, supported by a vector database and inference machinery, while the edge serves pages and static content via Cloudflare and Google backends.

sections.title: Evaluating models per site, for speed as well as accuracy
sections.summary: Model choice is treated as a per-site question rather than global. The team uses Promptfoo to evaluate prompts across many providers and models, including local and OpenAI-compatible ones, continuously because latency and accuracy depend on site size, vertical, and commerce type. Two criteria are tracked: accuracy and speed, since generation must complete in 1–2 seconds or conversions are lost.

sections.title: 1.1 seconds against 4.6
sections.summary: On the 15-prompt example site, Cerebras running Gemma 4 averaged 1.1 seconds of latency to generate a page, versus 4.6 seconds for the runner-up, with other configurations ranging from about 4 seconds upward. The decision rule is that a model is 'good enough' if it is fast enough, even if not perfect, and Sanchez reiterates that no frontier-scale LLM is needed because the work is selecting and arranging blocks.

sections.title: User signals, pre-generation, and personas
sections.summary: Browsing metrics—pages visited, time spent, persona bucket—feed the LLM and personalize the hero, products, blog feed, and navigation. A 'For You' recommendation page can be pre-generated as signals accumulate, trading latency pressure for higher compute cost from multiple LLM calls. Queries are also grouped into personas or intent types so marketers can define groups and the AI chooses blocks for each.

sections.title: Live demo: signals, buckets and a For You page
sections.summary: Sanchez introduces the 'audience of one' framing and walks through a fully generated coffee-machine example site. As he browses products and reads stories, a debug panel shows the user bucketed into 'exploring' with visited pages and time per page. A pre-generated 'For You' page is already available based on his browsing.

sections.title: Asking for a camping coffee machine
sections.summary: He runs a query for a coffee machine to prepare coffee while camping and the page is generated on the fly with camping-specific copy and recommendations such as the Aero and Pico. Debug mode shows 1.64 seconds total including a round trip to the LLM, with the LLM portion at about 1 second and throughput around 2,300 tokens/second on Cerebras Gemma 4.

sections.title: Swapping models on the fly
sections.summary: Because the demo site is shown to customers, controls let the presenter change models, temperature, and tokens to compare behavior. A second run is reported at roughly 1 second LLM time and ~2,200 tokens/second, which Sanchez describes as something 'we only dreamed about before.'

sections.title: Turning any URL into an Agentic Site
sections.summary: Beyond Promptfoo-driven evaluation, the OfOneLabs tool generates an agentic site for any URL in under an hour. Sanchez ran it on the AI Engineer site last week and demonstrates a query for 'Europe AI conferences' that returns AI-generated suggestions and a focused results page, plus a separate side-by-side comparison page generated on the fly for two conferences.

sections.title: Where this goes next
sections.summary: Sanchez sketches the future of intent-driven personalization: assembling a page per user via personal assistants, voice, and surfaces like Google TV, with no phone or computer required. He closes by projecting that this capability is now possible and will only become faster, cheaper, and more capable across multiple models, enabling large personalization options across sites and other surfaces.
